title: T-FREE: Subword Tokenizer-Free Generative LLMs via Sparse Representations for Memory-Efficient Embeddings
caption: Figure 1: Method comparison of classic Tokenization (left) and T-FREE (right) for text encoding (top) and decoding (bottom). Classic subword tokenizers learn a single-label vocabulary, i.e. a token is bijectively mapped into a single entry of the vocabulary. Instead, T-FREE uses a bijective multi-label mapping over multiple activations of hashed character trigrams. As T-FREE explicitly models morphological similarities, it enables compression of the embedding layer.
desc:
This figure presents an architecture diagram comparing two methods for text encoding and decoding: classic tokenization (left) versus T-FREE on the right. The top half illustrates how each method encodes input like "Hello_world!" into embeddings—classic uses single-word tokens with a fixed embedding size, while T-FREE aggregates hashed character trigrams through summation to form an aggregated representation of height h.

The bottom half shows decoding results using bar charts: on the left is a “single-class vocabulary” where each token maps uniquely (e.g., Sun or House), and on the right is a “multi-class vocabulary” that allows multiple tokens per activation, enabling morphological compression as shown by overlapping bars for words like mouse/ouse/house.

The figure visually demonstrates how T-FREE’s multi-label mapping over hashed trigrams enables more compact embeddings while preserving semantic similarity between related terms—such as sharing activations across word variants—which supports memory-efficient representation without sacrificing performance.

title: Pretraining with random noise for uncertainty calibration
caption: Fig. 2. Pretraining with random noise enables confidence calibration in neural networks.
desc: This figure presents multiple panels illustrating how pretraining with random noise improves confidence calibration and learning performance across different stages of neural network development: (a) shows a schematic comparing spontaneous activity before sensory input versus after eye opening; (b) displays timelines for visual and auditory system maturation from birth to adulthood, marking key developmental milestones like P0, P7, and P14. Panel (c) outlines the pretraining algorithm using random noise stimuli with Gaussian-distributed pixel intensities and uniform label distributions fed into a neural network architecture that outputs probability estimates over 10 classes; panel (d) compares test loss curves for models trained without versus with random preprocessing during early epochs, showing faster convergence when pretrained. Panels (e), (f), and (g) present histograms of confidence accuracy ratios, reliability diagrams comparing predicted vs actual performance against ideal calibration lines, and heatmaps visualizing error rates across network depths—demonstrating that pretraining leads to better-calibrated uncertainty estimates even with limited training data or shallow networks.
